2.2.1 SSTs

2.2.1.1 Jobs preparation

In order to prepare the Jobs of SSTs, the procedure described by Bosio et al. [67]
was followed. The main steps of the procedure are reported below:

    •  The powder was mixed with ethanol  at 50 % vol to  facilitate layer
       deposition, producing a slurry.

    •  The slurry was deposited on supporting disks with a diameter of 4 cm with
       the same powder material through a recoating system capable of controlling
       the layer thickness.

    •  The disks were heated up to 150 °C for 10 minutes to facilitate ethanol
       evaporation.

    •  The disk was placed in unique supporting platforms compatible with the
     LPBF machines to generate the laser tracks.

The powders used for SSTs production were Al4Cu and CL31. The Al4Cu powder
was an aluminum alloy gas atomized powder containing 4.5 wt% Cu, supplied by
the Universität Bremen. This powder was sieved below 50 µm and was processed
using an EOSINT M270 Dual mode system. The EOS machine is an industrial-
scale system equipped with a Yb-fiber laser with a maximum power of 200 W, a
wavelength of 1070 nm and a spot size of 100 µm. The building platform is 25 x
25 cm2, and the inertization of the chamber was achieved by Ar. The layer thickness
chosen for this powder was 50 µm. Materials and methods                                            56


The CL31 powder was supplied by GE Additive - Concept Laser. The powder was
sieved below 40 µm and was processed by Concept Laser Mlab cusing R. This
machine is a laboratory-scale system equipped with a fiber laser with a maximum
power of 100 W, a wavelength of 1070 nm and a spot size of 50 µm. The building
platform is 9 x 9 cm2, and the inertization of the chamber was achieved by Ar. The
layer thickness chosen for this powder was 25 µm.

In both powders SSTs Jobs scan speed and laser powder were varied to define a
proper process parameters window, producing an SST for each combination of
process parameters. In Figure 34 is represented the disk with the SSTs after printing.
Each “box” corresponds to a different combination of laser power and scan speed.





        Figure 34: Supporting disk with a diameter of 5 cm with SSTs on the top after
                                           printing.

2.2.1.2 Image Acquisition and elaboration

The instrument to acquire the images of the SSTs was a LEICA DMI 5000 M
optical microscope. For each SST, nine 100 x images were acquired to cover the
entire length of the track. The images at the track edges were excluded to avoid
errors in the measurements caused by border effects. In order to facilitate the post-
processing image analysis, the pictures were acquired, centering the SSTs as much
as possible. After gathering all the images acquired, the script can be run.

The script was implemented in ImageJ. More precisely, the script was written
through Fiji, a distribution of ImageJ, which includes a compiler environment, and
the language used was derived from Java script. The first step was the automatic
threshold to convert the greyscale image to a binary image (black and white). The
script works on the greyscale histogram of pictures to apply the binarization in the Materials and methods                                            57


same way for all images. This operation avoids acquisition errors and improves the
reliability of the measurements. The typical greyscale histogram of an on-top SST
is represented in Figure 35-a. After several tests, the script was set to detect the
minimum of the curve, observing that applying the threshold at this point would
achieve the best results in terms of SST border definition. After that, the images are
converted to binary images (Figure 35-b).

The last step was a further conversion from a binary image to a closed profile
characterizable by ImageJ in different ways. This profile is defined as a “region of
interest” (ROI), and is savable with the extension .roi. A representation of a ROI is
shown in Figure 35-c.





    Figure 35: Greyscale histogram of the pictures and minimum definition (a), on-top
SST image with binarization (b) and ROI representation (c).

The script is set with a regularity control which allows discarding the defective
SSTs. An SST is classified as “discontinuous” if there is more than one image
representing not closed profiles or “irregular” along the length. This situation
verifies with an important melt failure (Figure 36-a) or small substrate melts (Figure
36-b). On the other hand, if the images presented a closed profile, the SST is
classified as “regular” (Figure 36-c) and selected for further analysis. Materials and methods                                            58





        Figure 36: Optical pictures of “irregular” SSTs (a, b) and a “regular” one (c).

The script approach for the “regular” SST selection is schematized in Figure 37,
where an example of the process of 400 images, representing a complete SST job
characterization, is reported together with the processing time.





    Figure 37: Flowchart of the image elaboration by the script and processing time each
step

The next step represents the analysis of the ROIs of the regular SSTs by the script,
which is described in more detail in the next paragraph.

Abstract:

 This work aimed to get a better understanding of the behavior and melt cleaning efficiency of different commercial solid fluxes used in the foundry industry for the treatment of liquid aluminum alloys. This was realized by combining industrial melt treatment experiments with the application of characterization techniques that can provide information about the phase composition and thermal stability of different fluxes. Rotary degassing treatments coupled with flux addition using 5 different commercial fluxes were conducted on batches of EN AC-46000 alloy (AlSi9Cu3(Fe)) melt. The melt quality was assessed by the Qualiflash technique and Bifilm-Index (BI) analysis of reduced pressure test (RPT) samples. The phase composition and thermal behavior of the fluxes were investigated by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and differential thermal analysis (DTA), respectively. Among the 5 fluxes, two had a rather similar phase composition with the main constituents being NaCl, KCl, CaF2, MgF2, Na2CO3·NaHCO·3H2O, Na2SO4, and K2SiF6. These two fluxes, which contain a relatively high amount of fluoride components (about 11mol pct), and had a melting temperature below 600 °C, proved to be the most efficient in improving the melt quality. The Quality Temperature Index (QTI) values and normalized Bifilm-Index (NBI) results of the RPT samples generally showed a similar tendency, but there was only a loose relationship between the two parameters. Discrepancies between the results of different melt quality evaluation techniques can be traced back to their sensitivity to melt quality changes.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Corrosion remains a critical limitation in advanced engineering materials, particularly under aggressive and multi-environment conditions. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as promising candidates for corrosion applications due to their multi-principal-element design and their ability to form chemically complex passive films. However, a unified, mechanism-driven understanding of passive film behavior in HEAs remains lacking. This review systematically examines passive film formation, stability, and breakdown in HEAs. It further evaluates electrochemical characterization methods, identifies corrosion mechanisms in aggressive environments, and proposes design strategies to enhance corrosion resistance. A systematic review was conducted using the Scopus database following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. A total of 487 records were identified, of which 369 met the inclusion criteria. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and thematic classification was applied to identify dominant research clusters, mechanisms, and emerging trends. The findings show that corrosion resistance in HEAs is governed by multi-component passive films with complex chemistry and layered structures. Their performance is strongly dependent on composition, microstructure, and environment. Cr plays a dominant role in film formation, while Mo significantly enhances pitting resistance and stability in chloride- and acidic-environments. Electrochemical characterization consistently links low corrosion current density and high charge transfer resistance to stable passive films. Microstructural uniformity is also critical. Under aggressive conditions, including mixed-ion environments and tribocorrosion, degradation mechanisms shift from passivation-controlled behavior to dynamic film breakdown and repassivation. The ability of HEAs to rapidly reform passive films emerges as a key performance advantage. Future research should focus on multi-environment corrosion mechanisms, tribocorrosion behavior, and
                    <jats:italic>in-situ</jats:italic>
                    characterization of passive film evolution.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Bone defect repair is a complicated clinical problem, particularly when the defect is relatively large and the bone is unable to repair itself. Magnesium and its alloys have been introduced as versatile biomaterials to repair bone defects because of their excellent biocompatibility, osteoconductivity, bone-mimicking biomechanical features, and non-toxic and biodegradable properties. Therefore, magnesium alloys have become a popular research topic in the field of implants to treat critical bone defects. This review explores the popular Mg alloy research topics in the field of bone defects. Bibliometric analyses demonstrate that the degradation control and mechanical properties of Mg alloys are the main research focus for the treatment of bone defects. Furthermore, the additive manufacturing (AM) of Mg alloys is a promising approach for treating bone defects using implants with customized structures and functions. This work reviews the state of research on AM-Mg alloys and the current challenges in the field, mainly from the two aspects of controlling the degradation rate and the fabrication of excellent mechanical properties. First, the advantages, current progress, and challenges of the AM of Mg alloys for further application are discussed. The main mechanisms that lead to the rapid degradation of AM-Mg are then highlighted. Next, the typical methods and processing parameters of laser powder bed fusion fabrication on the degradation characteristics of Mg alloys are reviewed. The following section discusses how the above factors affect the mechanical properties of AM-Mg and the recent research progress. Finally, the current status of research on AM-Mg for bone defects is summarized, and some research directions for AM-Mg to drive the application of clinical orthopedic implants are suggested.

Abstract:
This paper is the continuation of our previous paper. In this work, we optimized the synthesis of aluminum borides by the SHS method. The purpose of the research was to develop the foundations of waste-free technology. The initial components were powders of boric anhydride (B2O3), aluminum (Al), the oxide-heating additive (KNO3), various fluxing additives, including mixed ones. Abstract:
The present study deliberates the recovery of sodium fluoride (NaF)-natrite (Na2CO3)-sodium chloride (NaCl) ternary fluxing agent from hazardous aluminum dross waste using three types of heating methods, including direct heating on a hotplate, heating by a drying oven, and microwave heating. Deionized water was used as a green solvent for the recovery experiments. Investigating the effects of time and temperature on recovery percentage showed that a recovery percentage of around 96.5% can be achieved under time and temperature of 90 min and 95 ℃, respectively. The recovered fluxing agent salt was characterized by XRD, FTIR spectroscopy, FESEM, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental analysis. Rietveld fitting analysis of phases detected in the XRD patterns showed that the recovered fluxing agent contained 74–81 wt.% NaF, 8–11 wt.% NaCl, and 11–14.7 wt.% Na2CO3. The FESEM micrographs revealed that the retrieved salts were in nano scale. The recovered fluxing agent showed different morphologies including needle-like, round shape, and a mixture of both, corresponding to microwave, drying oven, and hotplate heating methods, respectively. The nano-needles exhibited diameter of the tip and base in the range of 39–60 nm and 50–103 nm, respectively.

Abstract:
Copper nanoparticles (NPs) with an average particle diameter of 50–60 nm were successfully obtained by reducing an aqueous solution of a copper(II)-nitrilotriacetic acid complex with an aqueous hydrazine solution at room temperature under an air atmosphere. Copper NP-based nanopastes were printed onto a glass substrate using a metal screen mask and pressureless sintered under a nitrogen atmosphere at 200 °C for 30 min. The electrical resistivity of the resulting copper electrode was 16 μΩ · cm. For a metal-to-metal bonding test, copper nanopaste was printed on an oxygen-free copper plate, another oxygen-free copper plate was placed on top, and the bonding strength between the copper plates when pressureless sintered under a nitrogen atmosphere at 200 °C for 30 min was 39 MPa. TEM observations confirmed that highly crystalline metal bonding occurred between the copper NPs and the copper plate to introduce the ultrahigh strength. The developed copper NPs could provide promising advances as nanopastes for sustainable fabrication of copper electrodes and die attachment materials for the production of next-generation power semiconductors.

Abstract:
We have applied spark ablation technology for producing nanoparticles from platinum ingots (purity of 99.97 wt. %) as a feed material by using air as a carrier gas. A maximum production rate of about 400 mg/h was achieved with an energy per pulse of 0.5 J and a pulse repetition rate of 250 Hz. The synthesized nanomaterial, composed of an amorphous platinum oxide PtO (83 wt. %) and a crystalline metallic platinum (17 wt. %), was used for formulating functional colloidal ink. Annealing of the deposited ink at 750 °C resulted in the formation of a polycrystalline material comprising 99.7 wt. % of platinum. To demonstrate the possibility of application of the formulated ink in printed electronics, we have patterned conductive lines and microheaters on alumina substrates and 20 μm thick low-temperature co-fired ceramic (LTCC) membranes with the use of aerosol jet printing technology. The power consumption of microheaters fabricated on LTCC membranes was found to be about 140 mW at a temperature of the hot part of 500 °C, thus allowing one to consider these structures as promising micro-hotplates for metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) gas sensors. The catalytic activity of the synthesized nanoparticles was demonstrated by measuring the resistance transients of the non-sintered microheaters upon exposure to 2500 ppm of hydrogen.

From text 'gyarmati2025analysisofdifferent pages 2-4'.

Gábor Gyarmati, Ádám Pálóczi, Dorottya Somfai, Tibor Ferenczi, Tamás Mende, and Zoltán Kéri. Analysis of different commercial solid fluxes used during the rotary degassing melt treatment of casting aluminum alloys. Metallurgical and Materials Transactions B, 56:782-797, Dec 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-024-03376-9, doi:10.1007/s11663-024-03376-9. This article has 14 citations.

This excerpt does not provide the requested numerical before-and-after measurements for dissolved hydrogen (mL/100 g), bifilm index (mm), QualiFlash or spiral-fluidity values, oxide-inclusion counts, or pore numbers. It does establish the study’s treatment design and the conceptual distinction between degassing and oxide removal. Five commercial granulated fluxes were tested in an HPDC foundry using EN AC-46000 (AlSi9Cu3(Fe)) alloy. Each flux received three industrial treatment cycles; nitrogen was used at 20 L/min, 200 g of flux was added into the vortex, and the subsequent degassing phase lasted 300 seconds. Melt temperature averaged 740.2 °C before treatment and 699.9 °C afterward. Melt quality was evaluated using QualiFlash and reduced-pressure-test specimen image analysis, including bifilm-index assessment. The cited literature indicates that rotary degassing is broadly accepted for reducing dissolved hydrogen, whereas its ability to remove oxide inclusions is inconsistent and depends on process conditions and flux. In particular, the excerpt contrasts reports that pure-argon rotary degassing removed oxide films with the authors’ prior finding that nitrogen rotary degassing without flux was effective only for hydrogen removal. Thus, fluxing is presented as potentially important for inclusion/oxide removal, while gas degassing primarily addresses dissolved hydrogen; quantitative efficacy comparisons require results pages not included here.

Consequently, the excerpt supports the conclusion that rotary degassing is principally responsible for dissolved-hydrogen and porosity reduction, whereas fluxing contributes more directly to oxide/inclusion wetting, agglomeration, and removal into the dross. ## pqac-00000012

From text 'gyarmati2025analysisofdifferent pages 10-13'.

Gábor Gyarmati, Ádám Pálóczi, Dorottya Somfai, Tibor Ferenczi, Tamás Mende, and Zoltán Kéri. Analysis of different commercial solid fluxes used during the rotary degassing melt treatment of casting aluminum alloys. Metallurgical and Materials Transactions B, 56:782-797, Dec 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-024-03376-9, doi:10.1007/s11663-024-03376-9. This article has 14 citations.

The excerpt provides qualitative and process-related comparisons, but it does not report the requested before/after numerical values for dissolved hydrogen (mL/100 g), bifilm index (mm), Qualiflash fluidity or spiral-fluidity index, oxide-inclusion counts, or pore numbers. It states that fluxes B and D produced the greatest melt-quality improvements according to both Qualiflash and reduced-pressure-test (RPT) image analysis. These fluxes had similar NaCl–KCl compositions and approximately 11 mol% total fluorides, including single and double fluorides; the text attributes their superior oxide-removal performance partly to K2SiF6, which can dissolve oxide phases to a limited degree. Their melting temperatures were below 600 °C, allowing formation of a low-viscosity liquid that improves mixing and oxide wetting. In contrast, flux E melted at 715 °C, above the average post-treatment melt temperature of 699.9 ± 15.8 °C, and showed the lowest cleaning efficiency; Qualiflash even indicated poorer cleanliness after treatment. Thus, the excerpt supports a distinction between oxide-cleaning efficacy and degassing: it documents oxide-removal/melt-cleanliness trends, but gives no quantitative dissolved-hydrogen comparison or direct evidence here for separating degassing performance from oxide removal.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'gyarmati2025analysisofdifferent pages 1-2'.

Gábor Gyarmati, Ádám Pálóczi, Dorottya Somfai, Tibor Ferenczi, Tamás Mende, and Zoltán Kéri. Analysis of different commercial solid fluxes used during the rotary degassing melt treatment of casting aluminum alloys. Metallurgical and Materials Transactions B, 56:782-797, Dec 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-024-03376-9, doi:10.1007/s11663-024-03376-9. This article has 14 citations.

This excerpt describes an industrial study of EN AC-46000 (AlSi9Cu3(Fe)) melt treated by rotary degassing with five commercial solid fluxes. Melt quality was evaluated using Qualiflash/QTI and reduced-pressure-test Bifilm Index (BI/NBI), while flux phases and thermal behavior were characterized by XRD and DTA. Two fluxes were the most effective: both had approximately 11 mol% fluoride components, melting temperatures below 600 °C, and similar phase compositions containing salts and fluorides. The excerpt states that combined rotary degassing and flux addition effectively reduced oxide films and spinel-like inclusions, but it does not provide the requested numerical before/after values for dissolved hydrogen (mL/100 g), BI in millimeters, Qualiflash or spiral-fluidity indices, oxide-inclusion counts, or pore numbers. It also does not quantify the separate effects of argon degassing versus fluxing/oxide removal. Conceptually, the cited evidence distinguishes the functions: degassing targets hydrogen removal, whereas flux addition promotes inclusion/oxide separation; combined treatment can reduce both hydrogen- and bifilm-related defects. Results depended strongly on flux chemistry, and some fluxes could worsen melt quality. QTI and NBI followed broadly similar trends but were only loosely correlated because the techniques have different sensitivities to melt-quality changes.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'malisano2018quantitativestudiesof pages 46-51'.

J Malisano. Quantitative studies of gas porosity in cast aluminium & the determination of melt quality. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt provides background for interpreting, but not numerical before-and-after results for, Al-Si melt cleaning, fluxing, or rotary argon degassing. It explains that the Reduced Pressure Test (RPT) responds jointly to dissolved hydrogen and melt cleanliness, so an RPT-derived porosity measure cannot by itself distinguish hydrogen removal from oxide/bifilm removal. Vacuum expands gas pores and may unfurl bifilms; the resulting porosity is often used as an indicator of melt quality. The Bifilm Index (BI) is defined as the sum of pore lengths, with each pore length represented by its major axis, and it correlates with pore number. However, the excerpt cautions that hydrogen strongly increases pore size and therefore strongly affects total BI, meaning BI can change even without a corresponding change in bifilm population. The text identifies three RPT quantification approaches—bubble observation, Density Index, and cross-sectional pore examination—but gives no values for dissolved hydrogen in mL/100 g, BI in mm, Qualiflash or spiral fluidity, oxide inclusion counts, or pore numbers before and after treatment. It does state that degassing removes hydrogen by inert-gas bubbles, whereas inclusion removal involves flotation or sedimentation; inclusions with small entrapped air pockets may be neutrally buoyant and difficult to remove by holding alone.

Abstract:
Spherical powder materials are essential raw materials for manufacturing processes such as metal additive manufacturing and powder metallurgy. They possess characteristics that are key factors influencing the performance of additive manufacturing. This paper introduces the fundamental principles and characteristics of laser additive manufacturing technology and analyzes the technical principles, advantages, and disadvantages of three alloy powder preparation methods: gas atomization, centrifugal atomization, and plasma atomization. Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) has attracted significant attention in both the industry and academic fields since its inception, providing unprecedented advantages to fabricate complex-shaped metallic components. The printing quality and performance of L-PBF alloys are influenced by numerous variables consisting of feedstock powders, manufacturing process, and post-treatment. As the starting materials, metallic powders play a critical role in influencing the fabrication cost, printing consistency, and properties. Given their deterministic roles, the present review aims to retrospect the recent progress on metallic powders for L-PBF including characterization, preparation, and reuse. The powder characterization mainly serves for printing consistency while powder preparation and reuse are introduced to reduce the fabrication costs. Various powder characterization and preparation methods are presented in the beginning by analyzing the measurement principles, advantages, and limitations. Subsequently, the effect of powder reuse on the powder characteristics and mechanical performance of L-PBF parts is analyzed, focusing on steels, nickel-based superalloys, titanium and titanium alloys, and aluminum alloys. The evolution trends of powders and L-PBF parts vary depending on specific alloy systems, which makes the proposal of a unified reuse protocol infeasible. Finally, perspectives are presented to cater to the increased applications of L-PBF technologies for future investigations. The present state-of-the-art work can pave the way for the broad industrial applications of L-PBF by enhancing printing consistency and reducing the total costs from the perspective of powders.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Gas atomization is a key technology for producing high-quality metal powders, widely adopted in additive manufacturing and other powder-based industries due to its versatility and productivity. Its complexity, such as intense gas&ndash;liquid momentum exchange, thermal gradients in solidification, and multiple influencing factors, poses significant challenges for process control. This comprehensive review explores the complexities of gas atomization technology in metal powder production, examining the underlying mechanisms, simulation techniques, flow field dynamics, and key influencing factors. It clarifies that primary atomization is characterized by liquid film atomization, driven by Kelvin&ndash;Helmholtz instabilities, and fountain atomization, triggered by Rayleigh&ndash;Taylor instabilities. Secondary atomization, on the other hand, is predominantly influenced by shear and inertial forces. The review emphasizes the key roles of physical gas and liquid properties, temperature, pressure, nozzle design, and solidification processes in determining the characteristics of the resulting metal powder. It concludes that a thorough understanding of these factors is essential for refining the atomization process and improving the quality of the metal powder produced. The review suggests that future research should focus on resolving discrepancies in atomization mechanisms, enhancing simulation methodologies, and investigating the effects of advanced nozzle designs on the production of metal powder.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this technical paper, the oxidation mechanism and kinetics of aluminum powders are discussed in great details. The potential applications of spherical aluminum powders after oxidation to be part of the surging arresting materials are discussed. Theoretical calculations of oxidation of spherical aluminum powders in a typical gas fluidization bed are demonstrated. Computer software written by the author is used to carry out the basic calculations of important parameters of a gas fluidization bed at different temperatures. A mathematical model of the dynamic system in a gas fluidization bed is developed and the analytical solution is obtained. The mathematical model can be used to estimate aluminum oxide thickness at a defined temperature. The mathematical model created in this study is evaluated and confirmed consistently with the experimental results on a gas fluidization bed. Detail technical discussion of the oxidation mechanism of aluminum is carried out. The mathematical deviations of the mathematical modeling have demonstrated in great details. This mathematical model developed in this study and validated with experimental results can bring a great value for the quantitative analysis of a gas fluidization bed in general from a theoretical point of view. It can be applied for the oxidation not only for aluminum spherical powders, but also for other spherical metal powders. The mathematical model developed can further enhance the applications of gas fluidization technology. In addition to the development of mathematical modeling of a gas fluidization bed reactor, the formation of oxide film through diffusion on both planar and spherical aluminum surfaces is analyzed through a thorough mathematical deviation using diffusion theory and Laplace transformation. The dominant defects and their impact to oxidation of aluminum are also discussed in detail. The well-controlled oxidation film on spherical metal powders such as aluminum and other metal spherical powders can potentially become an important part of switch devices of surge arresting materials, in general.

Abstract:
Thin alumina coatings on Li-rich nickel cobalt manganese oxide (Li-rich NCM) particles used as cathode material in Li-ion batteries can improve the capacity retention during cycling. However, the underlying mechanisms are still not fully understood. It is crucial to determine the degree of coverage of the particle's coating on various length scales from micrometer to nanometer and to link it to the electrochemical properties. Alumina coatings applied on Li-rich NCM by atomic layer deposition or by chemical solution deposition were examined. The degree of coverage and the morphology of the particle coatings were investigated by time-of-flight secondary-ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS), scanning electron microscopy, elemental analysis using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry, and scanning/transmission electron microscopy. ToF-SIMS allows investigating the coverage of a coating on large length scales with high lateral resolution and a surface sensitivity of a few nanometers. Regardless of the chosen coating route, analytical investigations revealed that the powder particles were not covered by a fully closed and homogenous alumina film. This study shows that a fully dense coating layer is not necessary to achieve an improvement in capacity retention. The results indicate that rather the coating process itself likely causes the improvement of the capacity retention and increases the initial capacity.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminum recycling is pivotal for achieving carbon neutrality and advancing the circular economy, offering significant reductions in energy use and greenhouse gas emissions compared to primary production. This review synthesizes global advances from 2020 to 2025 in scrap collection, sorting, remelting, and alloy recovery, with a focus on technological progress, sustainability metrics, and policy integration. Secondary aluminum already supplies over one-third of global demand and could surpass 50 % by 2030 with stronger segregation systems and extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes. Innovations such as high-shear degassing, solid-state chip recycling, and chloride-free refining have improved melt quality and reduced salt-slag waste. At the same time, life-cycle assessments indicate up to 95% lower emissions compared to virgin aluminum. Persistent barriers remain—namely alloy contamination, inconsistent scrap classification, and limited traceability in informal collection networks. Regional policy experiences demonstrate that harmonized standards, mandatory recycled-content targets, and digital traceability accelerate market adaptation, whereas developing economies still face fragmented logistics and weak governance. Future directions include integrating real-time life-cycle assessment, artificial intelligence-based scrap sorting, and international alloy standards, enabling over 80% recycled content. Overall, aluminum recycling emerges as a technologically mature, economically competitive, and environmentally decisive route for decarbonizing metallurgical production and supporting the global energy transition.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Scrap-based melting is essential to the decarbonization of foundry production, but scrap selection is still often treated as a purchasing decision rather than as an integrated metallurgical design problem. This structured critical narrative review evaluated an audited corpus of 105 publications published from 2020 to August 2026. Evidence coding identified 40 aluminum-focused studies, 25 steel-focused studies, 7 cast-iron studies, 7 copper-alloy studies, 1 nickel-base study, and 25 cross-cutting contributions. Only 15 studies were industrial or pilot demonstrations, whereas 55 were laboratory studies and 35 were models, reviews, or contextual analyses. Nominal chemistry alone was consistently insufficient to determine scrap fitness: origin, size distribution, bulk density, coatings, oxide load, entrained contaminants, sampling uncertainty, and furnace-specific response jointly controlled metallic yield, energy demand, melt cleanliness, residual-element accumulation, emissions, and off-specification risk. The review proposes a normalized mass-balance formulation, probabilistic chemistry constraints, a cost-per-tonne-of-conforming-metal objective, and a four-gate scrap-to-alloy framework.</jats:p>

From text 'marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 84-90'.

F Marinucci. Development of alsi10mg based alloys for additive manufacturing processes. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt reports qualitative ONH results for self-atomized AlSi10Mg powders separated into <20, 20–50, 50–106, and >106 µm fractions, but it does not provide the numerical oxygen, nitrogen, or hydrogen values. ONH levels were generally similar across atomization runs and conditions. The <20 µm fraction had substantially higher oxygen, attributed to its greater surface area and oxidation tendency. The >106 µm fraction in RUN 1 also showed elevated oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen with high standard deviation, attributed to metallic scraps from the end of atomization; these scraps were less influential in RUN 3. The useful LPBF fraction was 20–50 µm. Its sieved yield was 67% for RUN 1, 46% for RUN 2, 49% for RUN 3, and 43% for RUN 4. Powders were predominantly spherical with smooth surfaces, but satellites were attached to larger particles. Agglomeration was most evident in RUN 3 and absent in RUN 4; the effect was considered undesirable for flowability, although sieving reduced fines. The excerpt does not discuss comparison with commercial CL31 powder or establish any correlation with recycled charge.

After the powder is produced and collected, the preliminary analysis is performed,
including weight to understand the atomization yield, PSD and SEM analysis. All

atomization process. After the gas flow is closed, some molten metal residual can
still be present in the crucible. Some drops of the molten residual can fall into the
atomization chamber, reaching the powder collector.

Process parameters optimization




The lab-scale atomization plant was successfully validated in Chapter 3 through the
production  of a good  quality powder, which  is highly comparable with a
commercial powder. The next step is to choose the right combination of process
parameters to produce bulk samples.

As already introduced in Chapter 1, the optimization of process parameters is a
procedure which can be carried out in several ways. This PhD thesis focuses on the
SST method, which can be very useful when a new powder must be tested,
especially when in the literature there is no baseline of process parameters to start.
The rapidity and easy performance of SST makes this technique perfect for this
purpose which  is a  critical point in new powder production and validation.
However,  this technique  presents  several drawbacks,  that make  the  results
unreliable.

The first part of Chapter 4 is dedicated to the SST method, with a study on the
traditional analysis methods, highlighting the main drawbacks. After  that, an
alternative method is proposed. This new method can overcome the main critical
issues of the SST approach and increase the analysis velocity. The main results in
this part were previously published in the work “An automatic on-top analysis of
single scan tracks to evaluate the laser powder bed fusion building parameters”
[117]. Then, the final optimization of CL31 and HM process parameters through
this new analysis method is reported. Process parameters optimization                                    82


The second part of this Chapter regards the bulk samples production of CL31 and
HM with optimized process parameters. In this part are present density analysis,

microstructure and mechanical properties, intending to finalize the comparison
between the powder and to understand if the powder self-produced is reliable after
the production of bulk components. Part of the result of these analysis were reported
in the previous work “Evaluation of a Laboratory-Scale Gas-Atomized AlSi10Mg
Powder and a Commercial-Grade Counterpart for Laser Powder Bed Fusion
Processing” [111].

4.1 SST: Traditional analysis of Al4Cu SST

The first SST analysis included on-top and cross-section observations of an Al4Cu
powder processed using an EOS M270 Dual Mode machine. The work of Bosio et
al. [66] was used as a baseline for the actual SST analysis since there a complete
study of SSTs produced with an EOS M270 Dual Mode was reported. Their
analyses included qualitative on-top observations of SSTs and measurements of the
main geometrical features of their cross-sections.

For Al4Cu, a similar analysis was reproduced. As described in Material and
Methods section, the single powder layer was obtained according to the procedure
reported by Bosio et al. [66]. Several process parameters were chosen to have a
complete idea of the melting and solidification behavior of SSTs with the variation
of laser power and scan speed. Figure 51 represents the on-top pictures and process
parameters. A color code was used to indicate the SST quality. Red indicates the
SSTs which presented evident defects in terms of discontinuity or “balling” effect.
For this reason, the corresponding process parameters must be excluded from the
selection. In green potential suitable parameters combinations are represented.
These parameters sets  produce SSTs that appears smooth and regular.

Considering this first analysis, it seems that the low power combinations must be
excluded from the selection probably because the energy supplied to the powder is
not enough to perform a correct melting. It seems that at least a power of 160 W is
necessary to obtain regular SSTs. Increasing the power (180 W and 195 W), all the
scan speeds can be chosen. However, the potential good parameters are still too
numerous to define a precise combination of process parameters. Process parameters optimization                                    83

2.6  The Reduced Pressure Test


  The Reduced Pressure Test (RPT), originally known as the Straube-Pfeiffer test, is

one of the oldest and simplest tests of metal quality that is still used extensively in many

casthouses. It was originally developed to measure hydrogen, but it was soon recognised

that it measured a convoluted combination of the melt hydrogen content and the melt

cleanliness together – hence it is often considered to be a straightforward test of melt

quality. It is precisely for this this reason, combined with its robustness, low cost, speed,

and simplicity, that the RPT finds extensive use.

2.6.1 Basic Principles

  The RPT involves taking a small sample of ~100g of metal and solidifying it under a

partial vacuum inside a vacuum chamber as shown in Figure 2.16 a). The application of

the vacuum magnifies the size of gas pores, making them visible to the unaided human

eye (Figure 2.16 b) ). The volume fraction of porosity is then considered to be inversely

proportional to the melt quality and the vacuum level. The vacuum level is selected based

on the melt quality and the amount of porosity that is expected, but is generally selected

to be of the order of either 100 mBar or 10 mBar (though this varies between commercial

instruments). For example, for a vacuum of 80 mBar (as used in this work), pores will be

expanded to ~12.5× of their atmospheric size according to the ideal gas law. If the

hydrogen level in the material is very high, selection of too low of a vacuum can result in

the pores blowing out of the top of the sample.

2.6.2 The RPT as a Bifilm Test

   In recent years the RPT has been increasingly used as a test for bifilms [9], [19], [65],

[75], [77], [93]–[95]. It is generally considered that application of the practical vacuum

during the RPT can be used as a means of unfurling and expanding them to form pores,

2.7  Melt Quality Control


   In order to control the hydrogen and inclusion content and keep the melt quality

within  specification, casthouses subject  their metal to a number  of pre-casting

treatments (as can be appreciated from Figure 1.1). Here, only two treatment processes

with relevance to this work will be covered; for an extended overview of the numerous

other melt quality control techniques, the reader is referred to the works of others [3]–

[5], [17].

2.7.1 Flotation & Sedimentation of Inclusions

  Melt holding is one of the most straightforward methods that can remove entrained

inclusions by floating or sedimenting them from the melt. Inclusions with a lower density

have a propensity to float, while those with a higher density have a propensity to sink

and sediment. The rate at which an inclusion moves through the melt during flotation or

settling is governed by Stokes’s law, and depends on its cross-sectional area and its

relative density difference to the melt [97].


  Oxide films have a slightly higher density that molten aluminium, which would

suggest that they would sink. However, the complex structure of oxide films, and

especially oxide bifilms, confound this reasoning as they may entrap pockets of air when

they are entrained in the melt. This in turn gives them a highly variable buoyancy. Those

with large pockets of entrapped air will float faster – as is the case with most dross –

however, those with small air pockets, may be essentially neutrally buoyant [6], which

means that holding will prove ineffective in removing them. Flotation may be facilitated

by bubbling gas through the melt, as the bubbles may collect suspended inclusions as

they pass through the melt and float them out. This way inclusions that would normally

                                                           Background

sink may be floated to the surface of the melt, where they may be entrapped by the dross

layer, which can simply be skimmed from the melt.


   TiB2 grain refiner (and endogenous (Ti,V)B2 [98]) particles have a tendency to

sediment out of the melt due to their much higher density (~4.5 g cm-3) compared to

molten aluminium, causing them to rapidly sink once added to the melt, though this is

highly dependent on the particle size [99]. As TiB2 settles through the melt, it may collide

with and build up on oxide films, which can facilitate their sedimentation. Once

sedimented, the melt above can be cast off, free of them.

the recovery yield. Undesired elements, as magnesium, strongly influence the results.
Thus the control of the charge is necessary. Metal yield varies among different scraps and
it is necessary to calculate it for each charge with a rigorous method. Charging method
has also to be defined and it must be equal for all tests. A variation of salt factor from 1.2
to 1.8 increases the recovery yield of more than 2 %. This result highlights the importance
of defining the optimum salt level, not only its composition. On industrial scale, this leads
to an increase of refined liquid metal. Energy and disposal costs related to the amount of
new salt have to be considered.

                                  4546Abstract

     The process used to obtain recycled Al alloys depends on the scrap quality. Rotary
furnaces are normally used in Europe as they allow a high productivity and they can
process low quality scrap using a salt flux to protect the molten metal from oxidation.
      In this article, the effect of the quantity of salt on the metal recovery has been
experimentally investigated melting different types of scrap under a mixture of NaCl-
KCl-Na3AlF6 salts. The quantity of salt has been related to the salt factor (SF), which is
the ratio between the non-metallic content in the scrap and the quantity of salt required.
The same levels of salt factor have been tested by melting the scrap in rotary and crucible
furnaces.
     The metal recovery increases with the salt content for both furnaces. The results
obtained with the different melting processes are comparable because the yield difference
is similar considering different salt factors. Crucible furnace gives greater metal recovery
but  it cannot replace rotary furnace in Al refining industry due to the lower melting
capacity. However, the results highlight that the optimization of the Al refining process
can be supported by preliminary tests through crucible furnaces reducing the time and
material consumptions.

                                     481. Introduction

     Aluminium is the most widely used nonferrous metal in the world being present in
sectors as diverse as transportation, packaging, construction, electricity and medicine. It
has grown to be a great competitor for engineering applications from the end of 19th
century when it became economically viable. The capacity of being recycled plays an
important role in increasing the aluminium spread.
     Recycled Al alloys offer economical and environmental advantages compared to
primary production: Rombach (1998) estimated an energy reduction from 174 GJ/ton to
20 GJ/ton while a reduction equal to the 95% of the CO2 emission is achieved according
to Das, Green, and Kaufman (2007).
     Their production starts from Al scrap, which is the core of the whole process. A
closed-loop recycling could be the best way to increase the effectiveness of the process,
as occurred for cans (Baeyens, Brems, and Dewil 2010), but it is not possible for all types
of scrap.
     Heterogeneity is an important aspect of scrap. It is clear that various categories of
scrap differ not only in their origin and composition, but also in the fraction of oxides and
other foreign materials. The quality of the charged scrap affects both the metal yield and
the metal recovery. The metal yield is the portion of a scrap consignment which becomes
useable metal after proper melting and can be used to estimate the metal content of the
scrap, while the metal recovery is defined as the percentage of metal gained from the
metal content of the scrap.
    An exhaustive classification of the Al scrap can be found in the EN 1676 (2010)
and EN 13920 (2003) standards where characteristics, chemical composition and metal
yield are provided for each category. The scrap quality is a key factor for the metal
recovery, thus different technologies have been developed to increase the obtainable
metal content. Comminution, sorting and de-coating are the main preliminary treatments
applied to the scrap.  Schubert, Sander, and Jackel (2004) highlighted that the aim of
comminution is to increase the scrap bulk density to favour handling and melting and they
also explained the fundamentals of this process. Several processes have been developed
to remove the non aluminium content of the scrap depending on the not wanted material,
as well summarized by Gaustad, Olivetti, and Kirchain (2012). The advantages of de-
coating is the reduction of the impurity coming from the scrap surface, in particular from
the organic fraction of the scrap coat as found out by  Kvithyld et al. (2008) through
thermal analysis on coated scrap.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'lopes2026recyclabilityinmetal pages 9-11'.

Ana Catarina Lopes, André F. V. Pedroso, Francisco J. G. Silva, Raul D. S. G. Campilho, Naiara P. V. Sebbe, and Rúben D. F. S. Costa. Recyclability in metal additive manufacturing: bridging powder lifecycle, defect evolution and fatigue-critical reliability across slm and ebm. Machines, 14:761, Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/machines14070761, doi:10.3390/machines14070761. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides measured oxide-thickness data for repeatedly reused AlSi10Mg powder, but it does not give a direct comparison between naturally air-grown oxide on atomized powder and oxide on a cast bar or ingot surface. Over 30 months of continuous powder reuse, the average uniform oxide layer reportedly increased from approximately 4 nm to 38 nm. Oxidized spatter particles developed a nodular oxide scale reaching up to 125 nm, attributed to extreme thermal exposure and approximately 1000 ppm residual oxygen in the build chamber. The associated bulk oxygen increase—from 500 ppm to 1250 ppm—reduced melt-pool wetting and promoted lack-of-fusion defects. For high-surface-area material, the excerpt identifies heavily oxidized spatter and irregular, coarser particles as important contributors to powder degradation, with altered reflectivity, increased defect density, and poorer flowability. The physical mechanisms described include vapor-recoil forces and melt-pool instabilities during laser melting, while surface tension competes with vapor pressure recoil to govern liquid-metal flow, spatter, and porosity. No quantitative oxide-loading comparison for atomized powder versus ingot/cast bar, nor a specific natural-air-growth thickness for those two surfaces, appears in these pages.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'rufino2007influenceofparticles pages 4-5'.

B. Rufino, F. Boulc’h, M.-V. Coulet, G. Lacroix, and R. Denoyel. Influence of particles size on thermal properties of aluminium powder. Acta Materialia, 55:2815-2827, May 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2006.12.017, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2006.12.017. This article has 162 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides measured oxide-shell thicknesses for atomized aluminum powders, but it does not specifically identify AlSi10Mg, compare atomized powder with a cast-bar surface, or report oxide thickness for an ingot or melt. HRTEM observations indicate that an as-prepared Al-1 particle consists of a crystalline aluminum core surrounded by an amorphous alumina shell approximately 3 nm thick. For sample Al-3, TEM of a focused-ion-beam section identified an amorphous oxide layer around 5 nm thick. The authors therefore used 3 nm as the oxide thickness for Al-1 and Al-2 and 5 nm for Al-3 in subsequent calculations. The excerpt also links powder surface area to particle-size distribution and nitrogen BET adsorption. BET and SEM-derived surface areas agree well for Al-1 and Al-2, while Al-3 shows a larger discrepancy attributed to surface roughness; this indicates that roughness can increase effective gas-accessible surface area beyond the geometric estimate. The text supplies a useful powder-oxide baseline and a mechanism for increased oxide loading in high-surface-area powders: smaller particles and rougher surfaces provide more surface per unit mass and therefore more alumina relative to bulk metal. However, no direct ingot/cast-bar comparison or melt oxidation kinetics are included.

The excerpt qualitatively reports that recycled/scrap addition increases oxide and inclusion content in aluminium, which reduces melt fluidity length and mould-filling ability. Pure A356 aluminium without scrap had higher fluidity than material containing 20% or 50% scrap. However, the excerpt does not provide the numerical fluidity fill lengths in centimetres or percentages, nor does it reproduce the values from Figure 2.5; it only states that fluidity decreased with scrap addition and that there was no apparent difference between 20% and 50% scrap. The proposed mechanism is physical flow restriction: oxides and inclusions block the metal-flow pathway, while also reducing effective superheat and hence metal flow. The text does not specifically discuss aluminium recycled dross, bifilms, or distinguish experimentally between bulk rheological fluidity and effective filtration/flow restriction. Its discussion therefore supports an interpretation that measured spiral-test fluidity/fill length can be reduced by entrained oxide/inclusion defects, but it does not quantify bifilm effects or separate intrinsic bulk fluidity from flow obstruction through a contaminated melt.

## pqac-00000042

From text 'pereira2026rotaryfurnacerecyclingof pages 16-19'.

Antonio Clareti Pereira. Rotary-furnace recycling of aluminum scrap and dross: a critical review of feedstock–flux–furnace interactions, metal recovery, emissions, and circularity. Journal International Review of Research Studies, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.66104/vnhbpj53, doi:10.66104/vnhbpj53. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt does not provide a primary quantitative relationship between recycled aluminum dross entrainment and melt fluidity, such as a fill-length change in centimeters or a percentage effect. It also does not report a direct casting-fluidity experiment distinguishing dross entrainment from other variables. Qualitatively, it identifies oxide films and envelopes as major flow and recovery barriers: entrained aluminum droplets may remain surrounded by oxide, requiring exposure, collision, drainage of the intervening film, and coalescence before recovery. Oxide-film formation is promoted by repeated deformation, fracture, folding, thickening, heating, stirring, and exposure to oxygen; high-surface-area feedstocks such as chips and foils are particularly vulnerable. The excerpt indicates that salt chemistry can modify oxide wetting, metal–salt interfacial tension, viscosity, and film disruption, while fluoride additions may improve coalescence but create environmental and corrosion penalties. It also notes that insufficient rotation preserves entrapped droplets. These mechanisms are relevant to fluidity, but the passage does not quantify bulk melt fluidity or fill length. Nor does it explicitly distinguish bulk fluidity—which concerns the overall flowability of the melt—from effective filtration or flow restriction caused by bifilms, oxide skins, entrained dross, or blocked flow paths. Such a distinction would require separate measurements.

The excerpt provides methodology relevant to filtration-based assessment of melt cleanliness, but it does not report the requested primary quantitative effect of recycled aluminum dross entrainment on bulk melt fluidity or fill length in centimeters or percent. The Qualiflash test evaluates how inclusions affect flow through a 15-ppi ceramic filter: dirtier metal causes filter clogging and reduces filling of a step-like mold, with the number of filled steps used to derive the Quality Temperature Index (QTI). QTI ranges from 1 for clean metal to 10 for highly contaminated metal. This is an effective filtration/flow-restriction measure, not a direct measurement of intrinsic bulk fluidity. The excerpt also describes reduced-pressure-test image analysis for pores and bifilms, including BiFilm Index, normalized BiFilm Index, pore number density, pore area fraction, and pore perimeter; however, it gives no results linking these quantities to fluidity or quantifying oxide/dross-induced flow reduction. Thus, the passage supports a distinction between inclusion-mediated filtration restriction and bulk fluidity, but supplies no numerical dross entrainment effect, no fill-length change, and no direct comparative evidence for bifilms or oxides beyond their implied role in melt contamination and pore formation.

Some of the factors which affect filling ability of a mould cavity are metal fluidity, metal

viscosity, pouring temperature, superheat, oxides and inclusions, backpressure, surface tension

and gating system (Voigt 2002). Below are brief discussions on how these factors plays a role

in the way the mould cavity is filled.

2.2.1 Metal fluidity


Fluidity shows how well the molten metal can flow into the entire mould cavity before freezing

(Rundma 2005). The higher the fluidity value, the higher the filling ability or the lower the

fluidity value, the lower the filling ability (Ding et al. 2013). Fluidity is measured with the use

of spiral test in millimetres (Campbell 1995). Possible defects which are associated with

inadequate flow are misrun and cold-shut (Ding et al. 2013).

2.2.2 Metal viscosity


Viscosity is a measure of how thick the metal is due to internal friction mostly caused by

applied force. It measures the fluid’s resistance to flow when force is applied (Sleigh and

Noakes 2008). Sleigh and Noakes (2008) states that viscosity is dependent on the temperature.

As temperature increases cohesive forces which hold the molecules together decreases and

movement of molecules increases, reducing viscosity. Pressure also affect viscosity of the

liquid because under high pressure, molecules need a lot of energy for interaction and this

makes viscosity to increase. Viscosity is inversely proportional to fluidity, the higher the

viscosity the difficult it would be for the molten metal to flow (Sleigh and Noakes 2008).

Viscosity can also be expressed as shear stress divide by shear strain as shown in equation 2.1;

2.2.3 Pouring temperature


The pouring temperature is an important parameter which indicates the energy content of the

liquid metal during the casting operation. It is normally taken as the sum of the liquidus

temperature and the superheat allowance which depends on the type of material being cast

(Rundman 2005). At low pouring temperature, molecules of the molten material are more

closely packed and rigid making it hard to flow the melt when force is applied. However, when

the pouring temperature is increased, the cohesion force which keep the molecules together

weakens up and molecules start to move more freely thus improving the fluidity of the molten

metal. When the pouring temperature increases, viscosity decreases, and the filling ability

increases. However, operating at high temperatures has its drawbacks which includes the

formation of shrinkage porosity, hot tearing and low mechanical properties (Li et al. 2015).

Castings produced at low pouring temperature tend to have globular-shaped fine grains while

castings produced at high pouring temperature have dendritic-shaped coarse grains (Ferguson

et al. 2014). This is a result of the low cooling rates associated with high pouring temperatures.


For instance, the filling ability of aluminium alloy was investigated at varying pouring

temperatures of between 680 °C and 750 °C with a die preheated to 50 °C by Ding et al. (2013).

Results showed low filling ability in the temperature range (680-730 °C) was attributed to high

viscosity and low pouring temperature. Increasing the pouring temperature to 740 °C, resulted

in a reduction in viscosity and an increase in filling ability. However, further increase in the

pouring temperature to 750 °C resulted in the formation of shrinkage defects at the thicker

sections of the casting (Ding et al. 2013).


When casting thin-walled sections, moulds need to be preheated before pouring to prevent

premature solidification (Anglada et al. 2013). However, this practice cannot be used in sand

moulds since their quality deteriorate with heat application (Anglada et al. 2013). For steels


                                                                         14with pouring temperature of about 1480 °C, moulds can be preheated to a temperature of about

1050 °C. This will reduce the heat transfer coefficient between the metal and the mould giving

enough time for metal to fill the mould cavity without premature solidification. This was also

noted by Zhang et al. (2009) who used a Low Pressure Die Casting (LPDC) process to cast a

thin-walled aluminium (A356 aluminium) of about 1.5 mm wall thickness. The results showed

an increase in filling ability of thin-walled section as pouring temperature and die temperature

increase. This is because an increase in pouring temperature reduces the solidification rate and

the metal will be hot for a long period of time to fill the entire mould cavity.

{"answer": "## Remelting Al–Si atomization returns: what the evidence supports

**Clean, compositionally matched returns can be remelted, but they are not equivalent to clean bar stock.** Chamber-wall splats, plate deposits, skull and off-specification powder bring pre-existing oxide skins into the charge; fines and thin splats present particularly large oxidized area per kilogram. Moisture can additionally supply hydrogen. The likely consequences are more dross and entrained oxide-film inclusions (*bifilms*), less reliable melt flow through restrictions, and potentially more metal lost during cleaning. These are metallurgical risks, **not measured percentage penalties for an Al 4047/AlSi12 or AlSi10Mg revert run**: the sources located do not provide a matched virgin-versus-revert atomization trial measuring melt oxygen, dissolved hydrogen, nozzle failures, powder morphology and final saleable yield together. Reuse of powder in a laser-printing machine is a different experiment from remelting that powder to make new powder. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000027)

### Quantitative reference points—and their limits

| Outcome | Reported observation | Interpretation for a *new atomization run* |
|---|---|---|
| **Melt oxygen and oxide films** | Salt-refining **off-specification Al–Mg–Sc powder**, not Al–Si, produced remelt blocks containing **192 and 454 ppm oxygen**, both below that alloy’s stated **500-ppm** limit. Metal recovery exceeded **85%** in both trials. Feed-powder oxygen was not reported, so neither an oxygen-removal percentage nor an untreated-revert comparison can be calculated. | Remelting fine powder *with effective oxide separation* can yield low-oxygen consolidated metal; simple remelting cannot be assumed to do so. Oxygen measured in a metal sample also does not independently count entrained bifilms. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000025) |
| **Hydrogen** | An industrial **AlSi9Cu3(Fe)** study found that rotary degassing reduced reduced-pressure-test density indices across the fluxes tested, consistent with hydrogen removal; it did **not** report a before/after dissolved-hydrogen concentration applicable to this revert charge. Its oxide-cleaning response depended on flux selection. | There is **no supported universal increment in mL H₂/100 g** attributable to remelting these returns. Measure dissolved hydrogen separately: a reduced-pressure porosity or bifilm index responds to *both* hydrogen and inclusions. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000036) |
| **Bifilms and restricted flow** | In that industrial study, starting inclusion-related melt quality varied with charge material; selected fluxes improved both filtration-based cleanliness and bifilm-related reduced-pressure-test measures, whereas one flux **worsened** the filtration-based result. Its **15-pores-per-inch** ceramic-filter test registers clogging and assigns a Quality Temperature Index from **1 (clean)** to **10 (contaminated)**. | Additional skins can become entrained films and obstruct a filter or narrow passage. This supports **increased clogging risk**, not a measured nozzle-clog frequency or a quantified change in intrinsic liquid viscosity. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| **Casting fluidity** | A published discussion of an **A356** casting comparison reports that **20% and 50% scrap** charges had shorter fluidity than **0% scrap**, with no apparent difference between the two scrap levels. The available text supplies **no defensible fill-length values**. | Reduced *casting fill length* is plausible with dirty returns; the example does not establish a 20% safe limit, a monotonic dose–response, or a value for AlSi12 atomization. Temperature, alloy chemistry and inclusion-mediated flow restriction must be distinguished. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000046) |
| **Oxygen of newly made AlSi10Mg powder** | In an **ingot-fed**, rather than revert-fed, gas-atomization comparison, laboratory powder contained **0.0287 ± 0.0007 wt% O (287 ± 7 ppm)** and commercial powder **0.0878 ± 0.0159 wt% O (878 ± 159 ppm)**. Their measured powder hydrogen contents were **20.1 ± 22.7 ppm** and **54.9 ± 0.942 ppm**, respectively. Finer size, passivation and subsequent handling were possible contributors; feedstock reuse was **not** the comparison. | Re-atomization does not necessarily reproduce either value. Specify and assay the *new powder*, including separate fine and target-size fractions; do not present the difference between these two suppliers as a revert effect. (pqac-00000021) |
| **Satellites, irregulars and yield** | The same ingot-fed AlSi10Mg trials produced mostly spherical powder **with satellites even without revert**. Total collected-powder yield was **62%, 79%, 88% and 78%** of the respective **1.5-, 3.1-, 1.5- and 3.1-kg** charges. The usable **20–50 µm** fraction was **67%, 46%, 49% and 43% of collected powder**, respectively—approximately **42%, 36%, 43% and 34% of the starting charges**, multiplying the reported fractions. A pressure discrepancy, not revert, helped explain the first run’s low total yield. | Satellites and reduced yield **cannot be attributed to revert solely because they appear in the next run**. No source establishes a numerical revert-induced increase in satellites, irregular particles, clogging events or loss of target-size yield across gas, ultrasonic and centrifugal atomizers. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000020) |

For comparison **only**, AlSi10Mg powder subjected to laser-printing use or deliberate aging—not remelted into a fresh atomization melt—rose from **0.067 to 0.072 wt% O** after one processing condition and from **0.067 ± 0.03 to 0.257 ± 0.07 wt% O** after **96 h at 400 °C in air**. Aging did not necessarily change particle shape, while oxidized spatter can add coarse irregular particles. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000032)

Electron microscopy measured approximately **3–5 nm** alumina shells on aluminum powders. For an **illustrative geometric estimate**, assume an intact, uniformly coated **30-µm-diameter sphere**, 3-nm Al₂O₃ film, aluminum density **2.7 g/cm³** and oxide density **3.05 g/cm³**. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028)"}

### How much oxide can powder or thin splats carry?

Electron microscopy measured approximately **3–5 nm** alumina shells on aluminum powders. Shell mass is then approximately **0.068% of the particle**, containing approximately **0.032 wt% oxygen, or 320 ppm**, *from that idealized film alone*. Its surface-to-mass ratio is approximately **0.074 m²/kg**. A **100-mm-diameter spherical bar/ingot**, given the *same* film, has about **3,300-fold less surface and pre-existing film per unit mass**; a **0.1-mm sheet or splat** coated on both broad faces has approximately **100-fold** the coated area per mass of the 100-mm sphere. Measured oxygen in an actual powder can differ substantially from this simple-shell calculation. (rufino2007influenceofparticles pages 4-5, marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 96-102)

### Practical disposition of returns

1. **Segregate and clean.** Keep same-alloy dense, clean returns separate from wall/plate deposits, crucible skull bearing refractory, dross, foreign-alloy particles and off-specification powder. Remove adherent dross, refractory and obvious contamination; clean the crucible, atomization chamber, collector and feed path between runs. In AlSi10Mg trials, particles of **304L steel** from a preceding run were detected in the next powder despite the changeover. Check alloy composition, particularly Mg, after refining: in the Al–Mg–Sc powder-recovery demonstration it fell from **4.6 wt%** in the feed to **0.25 or 0.95 wt%** in the recovered blocks. (marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 66-70, becker2021proofofprincipleofrecycling pages 4-6, marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 84-90)
2. **Keep returns dry and control fines.** Store covered and dry; verify drying/preheating appropriate to the equipment before charging, rather than introducing damp, loosely packed powder to molten aluminum. Separate very fine powder from dense returns and process it only by a validated route for high-surface-area material. In the AlSi10Mg atomization study, the **<20 µm** fraction carried substantially more oxygen than coarser fractions; off-spec **<25 µm** Al–Mg–Sc powder required a purpose-designed molten-salt recovery experiment. Fine aluminum powder also requires appropriate combustible-powder controls. (marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 84-90, becker2021proofofprincipleofrecycling pages 2-4, marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 66-70)
3. **Treat hydrogen and oxides as different problems.** If hydrogen is above the product-specific limit, use controlled inert-gas rotary degassing and **verify dissolved hydrogen**. Salt-refined fine-powder recovery used a **4:1 salt-to-powder** mass ratio, **2 wt% CaF₂** in equimolar NaCl/KCl and **750 °C**—an experimental recovery process, **not** a recommended routine atomizer charge recipe. 4. **Set revert fraction by qualification, not an invented maximum.** No credible general **maximum percentage of Al 4047/AlSi12 or AlSi10Mg atomization revert** is established by these studies. Begin with a separately characterized, preferably dense/clean return class and a conservative trial blend; increase its fraction **only while** melt hydrogen and inclusion/filtration tests, alloy chemistry, nozzle-flow continuity, new-powder oxygen and size-specific saleable yield remain within the operation’s documented virgin-charge limits. Account for dross, skull, uncollected powder and out-of-size powder separately rather than calling all collected material product yield. (marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 70-73, marinucci2023developmentofalsi10mg pages 84-90, gyarmati2025analysisofdifferent pages 5-7, mugeri2018optimisationofcasting pages 31-35)

**Bottom line:** Reverting clean Al–Si metal is feasible, but oxidized high-area returns make melt cleanliness and recovery a qualification issue. contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative evidence about recycled AlSi10Mg powder used in laser powder bed fusion, but it does not report remelting aluminum-silicon atomization scrap into new powder. For powder reuse, Raza et al. observed 30 months of continuous reuse: oxidized spatter increased to 3% by volume, the average oxide layer thickened from approximately 4 nm to 38 nm, and bulk oxygen rose from 500 ppm to 1250 ppm. Individual spatter particles developed nodular oxide scales up to 125 nm thick. These changes reduced powder-bed wetting and were associated with lack-of-fusion defects. The excerpt also reports that recycled powder can produce parts with microstructures, yield strength, and tensile strength comparable to virgin powder, although build-direction anisotropy remained. Lutter-Günther et al. linked spatter to vapor-recoil forces and melt-pool instabilities; the resulting particles had irregular morphology, greater surface oxidation, and often coarser microstructures than virgin powder, impairing flowability and increasing defect risk when reused. No quantitative data are provided here for melt hydrogen concentration, oxide inclusions in remelted feedstock, atomizer nozzle blockage, atomization yield, or powder production from AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, or 4047 scrap. Thus, the evidence concerns additive-manufacturing powder reuse and degradation, not feedstock remelting and atomization.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes an industrial study of EN AC-46000 (AlSi9Cu3(Fe)) melt treated by rotary degassing with five commercial solid fluxes. Melt quality was evaluated using Qualiflash/QTI and reduced-pressure-test Bifilm Index (BI/NBI), while flux phases and thermal behavior were characterized by XRD and DTA. Two fluxes were the most effective: both had approximately 11 mol% fluoride components, melting temperatures below 600 °C, and similar phase compositions containing salts and fluorides. The excerpt states that combined rotary degassing and flux addition effectively reduced oxide films and spinel-like inclusions, but it does not provide the requested numerical before/after values for dissolved hydrogen (mL/100 g), BI in millimeters, Qualiflash or spiral-fluidity indices, oxide-inclusion counts, or pore numbers. It also does not quantify the separate effects of argon degassing versus fluxing/oxide removal. Conceptually, the cited evidence distinguishes the functions: degassing targets hydrogen removal, whereas flux addition promotes inclusion/oxide separation; combined treatment can reduce both hydrogen- and bifilm-related defects. Results depended strongly on flux chemistry, and some fluxes could worsen melt quality. QTI and NBI followed broadly similar trends but were only loosely correlated because the techniques have different sensitivities to melt-quality changes.

ONH levels were generally similar across atomization runs and conditions. The <20 µm fraction had substantially higher oxygen, attributed to its greater surface area and oxidation tendency. The >106 µm fraction in RUN 1 also showed elevated oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen with high standard deviation, attributed to metallic scraps from the end of atomization; these scraps were less influential in RUN 3. The useful LPBF fraction was 20–50 µm. Its sieved yield was 67% for RUN 1, 46% for RUN 2, 49% for RUN 3, and 43% for RUN 4. Powders were predominantly spherical with smooth surfaces, but satellites were attached to larger particles. Agglomeration was most evident in RUN 3 and absent in RUN 4; the effect was considered undesirable for flowability, although sieving reduced fines. contexts.context: The excerpt experimentally compares virgin AlSi10Mg powder, once-processed/reused powder (R0), powder aged for 96 h, and R0 powder aged for 96 h. It reports morphology for the nominally 20–63 μm powder range: particles remained predominantly near-spherical, with occasional irregular or elongated particles, and no significant shape change was detected. R0 processing did not alter particle size (D50 39.8 μm virgin versus 39.9 μm R0), whereas aging increased D50 to 43.1 μm, interpreted as powder coarsening. Surface oxidation was the main morphological change: small oxide nodules were seen on R0, while aged states showed dark oxide nodules attributed to non-homogeneous growth of a γ-Al2O3 layer. The excerpt quantifies an approximately 15% reduction in laser absorbance from virgin to aged 96 h powder, with average absorbance declining from 68.55% to 58.23%; R0 remained similar to virgin at 68.48%, while aged R0 was 58.13%. It discusses oxygen content qualitatively but provides no numerical oxygen or hydrogen concentrations. It also contains no evidence concerning remelting scrap, so aging/reuse cannot be quantitatively distinguished from scrap remelting using this excerpt alone.
contexts.question: Quantify experimentally the influence of 20-63 micron AlSi10Mg powder aging or reuse on oxygen and hydrogen concentrations in powder and on powder morphology; distinguish from remelting scrap.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides experimental evidence for AlSi10Mg powder reused six times in a selective laser melting process, with a nominal original particle-size range of 20–63 µm. It reports that the aluminum-alloy powders, including AlSi10Mg, have wider particle-size distributions and greater variation in particle size than the studied Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V powders. Reused powders contain fewer fines, attributed to sieving out sintered particle agglomerations; the setup used a 100-µm sieve. Reuse is also associated with satellite formation because smaller particles can melt and sinter onto larger particles. Among the materials examined, AlSi10Mg is described as having the least homogeneous particle shape. The oxygen measurements used LECO analysis, based on averages of three measurements with approximately 0.19 g per sample. Oxygen differences between virgin and used powders were generally not appreciable, but AlSi10Mg was the exception: its oxygen content “almost doubles” from the initial value. The excerpt gives no hydrogen measurements or concentrations, and it does not provide numerical morphology metrics or oxygen values for AlSi10Mg. It also discusses powder reuse rather than remelting scrap, so the supplied passage cannot distinguish aging/reuse effects from remelting scrap effects experimentally.
contexts.question: Quantify experimentally the influence of 20-63 micron AlSi10Mg powder aging or reuse on oxygen and hydrogen concentrations in powder and on powder morphology; distinguish from remelting scrap.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that aging of AlSi10Mg powder—whether during storage or recycling—introduces additional oxygen and hydrogen, while producing no significant change in particle size or morphology. Thus, for the stated 20–63 µm powder fraction, the experimentally supported morphological conclusion is that aging preserves the powder’s particle-size and shape characteristics, whereas its chemical condition deteriorates through oxygen and hydrogen uptake. The excerpt does not provide numerical oxygen or hydrogen concentrations, nor does it specify concentration changes for a particular 20–63 µm batch. It also does not present a direct comparison between aged/reused powder and remelted scrap. The text distinguishes powder aging/recycling as exposure-related phenomena: metal powder is highly susceptible because of its high surface-to-volume ratio, and oxygen and hydrogen exposure can occur mainly during storage or powder recycling. Oxygen-related oxidation reduces powder laser-beam absorbance and affects melt-pool wetting and track geometry. Hydrogen is identified as a principal cause of porosity in deposited aluminium, because its solubility drops sharply during solidification. Therefore, the excerpt supports a qualitative distinction—aged or reused powder gains oxygen and hydrogen without major morphology changes—but quantitative concentration values and evidence concerning remelting scrap require other portions of the article or a separate source.
contexts.question: Quantify experimentally the influence of 20-63 micron AlSi10Mg powder aging or reuse on oxygen and hydrogen concentrations in powder and on powder morphology; distinguish from remelting scrap.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a qualitative-to-partly quantitative assessment of AlSi10Mg powder aging and reuse, but it does not provide the requested numerical oxygen and hydrogen concentrations for a 20–63 μm fraction. Aging from handling, storage, laser exposure, and recycling introduced oxygen and changed powder chemical and morphological characteristics, including surface appearance and reduced laser absorbance. The reported downstream effect was higher pore occurrence in parts made from aged powder: 6.5% porosity versus 3.16% for virgin powder. The introduction cites prior reuse studies in which repeated processing generally increased oxygen content, while oxidation was associated with thick Al2O3 and MgAl2O4 surface products. It also notes that humid storage physically adsorbed water, removable by drying, whereas the oxygen increase remained largely unchanged, suggesting a persistent oxide layer. No hydrogen measurements or hydrogen concentrations are reported in the provided excerpt, and no numerical particle-morphology metrics are given. The material discussed is powder used and recycled in laser powder bed fusion; remelting scrap is not addressed, so the excerpt cannot distinguish powder aging/reuse effects from remelting-scrap effects experimentally. The 20–63 μm size range is likewise not specified in these pages.
